narrative:
The model estimates a 15% chance that you will fail your final year. That is a low but not negligible risk: most students with this profile are expected to pass, but the school treats a one-in-seven risk as enough to require remedial courses so a small risk does not become a lost year.

The three strongest signals in your profile all worked in your favour, lowering the estimated chance of failure. The most influential was your record of past class failures: you have none, matching the passing average, so this was protective. The next was your intention to pursue higher education; wanting to continue studying is strongly linked with passing. The third was your low amount of free time, which also leaned toward passing rather than failing.

Because those top signals are favourable, the remaining risk comes from practical pressures. You reported under two hours of weekly study, while most passing students report two to five, and your eight absences are well above the passing average of about four. A 30–60 minute journey to school, much longer than most passing students’ under-15-minute trip, may add strain. To improve, protect a regular study block, reduce avoidable absences, and ask for help early; use your clear strengths—no past failures and a wish to continue education—as your foundation.
